History:
• 28-year-old man presents with “bad diarrhoea” for 3 days.  
• Frequency 4–5 loose/watery bowel motions per day; variable consistency.  
• Mild lower-abdominal discomfort; single episode of vomiting; possible low-grade fever.  
• Mildly reduced appetite but able to tolerate oral fluids; denies dehydration symptoms.  
• No blood or mucus in stool.  
• No recent travel, unusual foods, or known sick contacts.  
• Similar but self-limited episodes previously after certain foods/travel; none recently.

Past Medical History:
• Asthma (current).  
• Medications: “Lexapro” inhaler – dose/route/frequency not documented (name likely incorrect; clinician uncertain). No other regular medicines reported.  
• Allergies: Denies drug allergies.  
• Family history: Father hypertensive; died of bowel cancer at age 62.  
• Social history: Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
• General: Appears well; clinician notes “doesn’t look dehydrated.”  
• Mental status: Alert, oriented, conversant.  
• Abdominal exam, vitals, mucous membranes, skin turgor: Not recorded.  
• Other systems: Not recorded.

Impression:
Acute self-limited infectious gastroenteritis, most likely viral.  
DDx consistent with transcript:  
1. Acute viral gastroenteritis – typical 3-day watery diarrhoea, mild systemic features.  
2. Acute bacterial food-borne gastroenteritis – possible, though no clear exposure.

Management Plan:
• Supportive care emphasized.  
  – Maintain high oral fluid intake.  
  – Start oral rehydration salts (Dioralyte) as needed.  
• Dietary advice: “Soft” bland diet (toast, crackers, mashed/boiled vegetables).  
  – Avoid dairy (except yoghurt/probiotics), meat, fish, and eggs until 48 h diarrhoea-free.  
• Red-flag instructions:  
  – Seek care if stools > 6–8/day, blood in stool, persistent diarrhoea > 1 week, signs of dehydration, or high fever.  
  – If blood appears or symptoms ≥ 1 week, arrange stool sample ± antibiotics evaluation.  
• Documentation placed in patient’s app for review.  
• No medications prescribed at this time.

Patient Summary:
Young man with a short course of watery diarrhoea, mild abdominal pain, and minimal systemic upset, most consistent with viral gastroenteritis. Supportive management and dietary modifications advised; instructed on warning signs and when to seek further care.

Key Takeaways:
• Drink plenty of water and add oral rehydration salts to replace lost fluids.  
• Follow a bland, easily digested diet and reintroduce meat/dairy only after 48 h without diarrhoea.  
• Contact the service or seek urgent care if bleeding, > 6–8 stools per day, dehydration signs, or no improvement within one week.

Next Steps:
• Monitor symptoms at home; review notes in app for guidance.  
• Return for reassessment or stool testing if red-flag features occur or symptoms persist beyond 7 days.

Quality checks:
• Missing elements: No vital signs, physical abdominal findings, smoking/alcohol history, complete medication reconciliation (inhaler name/dose unclear).  
• Conflicts: Patient states “Lexapro” inhaler (antidepressant name vs asthma inhaler) – conflict noted.  
• Transcript quality: Clear overall; occasional inaudible words but key clinical details obtainable.
